individual_physics_teacher_note: Moving downward at constant terminal speed means net vertical force is zero, NOT that all forces vanish. In the simplified two-force model upward drag balances weight; buoyancy could also contribute to force balance.
Opening a canopy can make upward drag exceed downward weight, producing upward acceleration while the parachutist still moves DOWN. This is ordinary aerodynamic drag, not Stokes small-sphere drag.
At steady descent after canopy deployment, net force zero; drag ≈ weight in the simplified model, although buoyancy is physically present and usually small relative to weight.

Prepared-source question cites the before-canopy horizontal segment of Figure 6.5(c); a horizontal downward speed–time segment represents constant downward speed, not zero velocity. GitHub links unit6-figure65c, but the exact original printed NBF figure geometry, plateau position and caption have not been directly inspected in this review.

review_theme: Parachute time-since-jump and original textbook attribution
individual_physics_teacher_note: From stated values 42 s + 5 s = 47 s after jump, source D. The 42-second deployment and next 5-second transition are teacher-prepared textbook-attributed values; original printed NBF Figure/Example pp.91–95 is still unverified. This is approximate, not a separately timed measurement.
Given 50 m/s before and 8 m/s after canopy, ratio is 50/8=6.25, dimensionless. Does not mean velocity becomes zero when canopy deploys.

Honey generally has greater viscosity and drains more slowly than water with sufficiently comparable temperature, fill, head, cup geometry and flow arrangements. Identical cups alone do not guarantee all other conditions identical.

review_theme: Heating liquid and lowering dynamic viscosity
individual_physics_teacher_note: For ordinary syrup and many other liquids, warming generally reduces dynamic viscosity, improving pouring. Do not treat as universal for all phase-changing/non-Newtonian materials.
Most ordinary gases exhibit increasing viscosity with temperature under typical conditions; the stem specifically limits itself to cases following the usual trend.
In a sufficiently good vacuum, ordinary liquid/gas drag is effectively absent; other possible forces can remain, but this question is about fluid drag only.

review_theme: Zero motion drag does not remove buoyancy
individual_physics_teacher_note: A sphere at rest relative to still liquid has zero motion-related Stokes drag because v_rel=0; hydrostatic buoyancy and weight can still act, with support if necessary.

review_theme: Figure 6.3 exact attribution and geese formation
individual_physics_teacher_note: Prepared master attributes energy/drag savings in V flight to NBF Figure 6.3; the existing public source refers to unit6-figure63. Exact printed figure/caption not directly inspected here. Benefits depend on positioning, wake/upwash interaction and roles; do not promise every bird always receives identical drag reduction.
With comparable air speed, turning a broad palm edge-on generally reduces projected area and drag. This example is conceptual; students should not extend hands outside a moving vehicle.

review_theme: Droplet size and Stokes terminal speed
individual_physics_teacher_note: Under the simplified low-Reynolds Stokes model v_t∝r², so a smaller same-material droplet has lower model terminal speed. Real droplets may be outside creeping-flow regime.

review_theme: Viscosity comparison confounded by different fluid densities
individual_physics_teacher_note: Source answer D (half terminal speed) follows v_t∝1/η only when ALL other terms are fixed, especially sphere density, fluid density/buoyant density difference, radius, g and creeping-flow conditions. Saying only 'fluids of different viscosity' and 'same Stokes assumptions' does not explicitly fix density; different fluids may have different buoyancies. Clarify that equal other variables/identical fluid density are assumed before certified exam reuse.
Fast full-sized parachutes are neither tiny rigid spheres nor low-Reynolds creeping flows; they need a more suitable general aerodynamic drag treatment. Option C remains supported.
Neglecting buoyancy and any other vertical force: W−F_d=20−12=8 N DOWNWARD; this sets downward acceleration, not necessarily instant velocity direction.

900 N upward drag minus 700 N downward weight gives 200 N upward net force if no other vertical forces are significant. For a parachutist currently falling DOWN, upward acceleration DECREASES the downward speed; velocity does not become zero instantaneously.

review_theme: Zero acceleration is not zero velocity
individual_physics_teacher_note: A body at terminal downward speed is still moving at constant nonzero speed; net force/acceleration are zero under the chosen simplified model.

Given teacher-master values η_milk=2.12 mPa·s and η_ethanol=1.144 mPa·s, ratio is 2.12/1.144≈1.85315≈1.85, original D. Both units cancel. Exact NBF Table 6.1 numbers and 20°C source attribution still need direct printed-textbook verification.
